cells.tense: You are standing here with your hands in it, learning how the thing in front of you actually grows.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what is not
cells.ask: Take something you've grown that's finished — ripe, complete, past where your attention changes it. Stop watering it. Put your hands back on what's still coming up; the finished one stays finished.
cells.core:
You're good at tending, and the care has a shape: patient, hands in the dirt, watching what makes a thing come up. That's a real skill. In a place where things get weighed back level, the skill has a limit built in — some things you've grown are done growing, and the care that made them can't tell the difference between ripe and unfinished.

So take one that's finished. Done, complete, past the point where your attention changes anything. Stop watering it and put your hands back on what's still coming up. Releasing it isn't the end of the care; it's proof the care worked. The next thing gets your whole hand, not the part still holding the last one. You'll feel the difference in how much of you is available.
cells.sheetLine: What you tend is ripe and you're still watering it.
cells.verb: learning how a living thing actually grows by tending it
cells.place: where what's out of proportion gets weighed back level

cells.tense: Something in you is already weighing next season's fairness, bracing against a scale that hasn't tipped yet.
cells.act: sense what has not happened yet, with wonder
cells.ask: Before you rule on whether something will even out, sit with it and feel where it's headed — sense it, no verdict. Wonder what it might become instead of costing it out first.
cells.core:
You can feel a thing's future before it arrives, and lately the feeling is doing the deciding. Where something lands near you, your attention has gone to the part that hasn't happened yet — next week's fairness, next month's balance, whether the people involved come out even. Care aimed at next season runs out faster than care spent on this one.

So before you rule on something, sit with it and feel where it's actually headed. Not the verdict — the direction. Wonder what it might become instead of calculating what it will cost. Once is enough to find out whether the bracing was needed. If it was, you'll see it more clearly. If it wasn't, you'll know. The verdict can wait a day; your shoulders already answered the question.

cells.tense: You were tending something that got set down partway, and you haven't gone back to it.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Begin something this week for no reason but the beginning itself — a seed, a page, a first step. Plan nothing past the first move, and don't decide yet if you'll continue.
cells.core:
There's something you were tending that got set down partway, and after that the hands got quiet. The balance here isn't yours to call anymore, and calling it was the part that used to feel like yours. Restoring it feels like too much to pick up, so nothing gets picked up, and the room stays off-kilter while you wait at the edge.

What revives this isn't pushing into the flat place. Begin something this week for the plain pleasure of beginning it — a seed, a page, a first walk. No plan beyond the first move. It doesn't have to fix anything. Beginning one thing teaches you that starting is still available, and the thing that got set down can wait until your hands come back.
cells.sheetLine: You set it down halfway and haven't gone back.

cells.tense: The balance around you is kept, day after day, by hands you don't count as doing it.
cells.act: drop one condition you set and take the step
cells.ask: Pick a worry you've been holding steady for someone and give it to them — name it, then leave it with them this week. Take the step once the condition goes.
cells.core:
You keep things level for the people near you and then talk about it like it happens without you. Somebody's rough week gets smoothed, somebody's load gets lightened, somebody's schedule gets adjusted — and the story is that you weren't really involved. The work happens. The credit for doing it goes to nobody, including you.

So drop one condition: that it only counts if you carry it silently. Pick a worry you've been holding steady for another person and give it to them, with a time and their name on it. Don't explain why. Let one thing be theirs for a week. What you've been carrying alone becomes visible, and you find out what it weighs when it leaves your hands.
cells.sheetLine: The balance is kept by hands you don't count.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person is measuring fairness against some scoreboard — the record only says care is happening through Structure in a seat of calibration, not that anything is being counted. A reader could reasonably say they never think in terms of fairness at all; the ask still works because tending one thing through to done is useful whether or not the reading is right, and the person learns where their care actually lands. The sentence that serves me more than them is the Too Little opening about a door already behind them — I cut the second person and the drama and left only what a camera could see: something tended halfway and set down.
